cards.b: The muscle that contracts to produce movement at a joint.
The muscle that relaxes and lengthens to allow the agonist to move the joint.
A muscle that stabilises a joint or body part so the agonist has a firm base.

cards.f: Agonist and antagonist for elbow flexion
cards.b: Biceps is the agonist; triceps is the antagonist.

cards.f: Agonist and antagonist for knee extension
cards.b: Quadriceps is the agonist; hamstrings is the antagonist.
Muscle shortens while contracting, e.g. biceps lifting in a curl.
Muscle lengthens while contracting, e.g. biceps lowering the weight.
Muscle contracts without changing length and there is no movement, e.g. holding a plank.
Slow, fatigue-resistant, aerobic, red. Suit marathon and endurance sports.
Fastest, most forceful, anaerobic, tire quickly. Suit 100 m sprint, weightlifting.
Fast and powerful, moderately resistant to fatigue. Suit 400 m, 800 m, team sports.
An increase in the size of muscle fibres from training.
Large back muscle; pulls the arm down and back (adduction), e.g. pull-ups, butterfly.

cards.f: Pectoralis major: where and sport use
cards.b: Chest; brings the arm across the body, e.g. bench press, throwing.

short.q: Explain why muscles work in antagonistic pairs.
short.model: Muscles can only pull, not push, so one muscle contracts to move the bone and its pair relaxes. The pair then reverses the movement.
points: one contracts while the other relaxes

short.q: Describe the muscle actions at the elbow during the upward and downward phases of a bicep curl.
short.model: Upward: biceps contracts concentrically and triceps relaxes. Downward: the biceps lengthens under control (eccentric) as the weight lowers.

short.q: Explain why a 100 m sprinter benefits from fast glycolytic fibres.
short.model: They contract quickly and produce high force for powerful short bursts, using anaerobic energy, which suits a race of about 10 seconds.

short.q: Name the muscle that pulls the toes up (dorsi flexion) and explain when a runner uses it.
short.model: Tibialis anterior. It lifts the toes so the heel strikes first as the foot lands.

short.q: Give an example of an isometric contraction in sport and explain why it is isometric.
short.model: Holding a handstand in gymnastics: the muscles contract against the load but do not change length and there is no movement.
points: no change in length / no movement
